summary: Incident to development (I2D) is the U.S. tax concept that captures research-related support, supervisory, and indirect costs under IRC §§ 174 and 174A. For the IRC § 41 research credit, it works through first-line direct supervision and direct support wages; if an employee's qualified services reach 80% of their time, 100% of their W-2 wages qualify as QREs.

body.text: Incident to development (I2D) is the U.S. tax concept that captures research-related support, supervisory, and indirect costs under IRC §§ 174 and 174A. For the IRC § 41 research credit, it works through first-line direct supervision and direct support wages; if an employee's qualified services reach 80% of their time, 100% of their W-2 wages qualify as QREs.

The concept of expenditures "incident to the development or improvement of a product"—referred to in practice as Incident to Development (I2D)—serves as the primary regulatory bridge between broad research and experimental (R&E) accounting under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) §§ 174 and 174A and the narrower calculation of Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) for the federal Credit for Increasing Research Activities under IRC § 41. While Treasury Regulation (26 CFR) § 1.174-2(a)(1) broadly encompasses all direct and indirect costs incident to eliminating technical uncertainty regarding a product's capability, method, or appropriate design, IRC § 41(b) restricts credit-eligible in-house expenses to employee wages for "qualified services," tangible non-depreciable supplies, and qualified off-premises computer time-sharing. Consequently, within the IRC § 41 regime, the economic leverage of the "incident to development" concept operates primarily through IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)–(d), which include "direct supervision" (immediate first-line management) and "direct support" of qualified research within the statutory definition of qualified services. Under the "substantially all" rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2), if an employee's qualified services—combining hands-on experimentation with direct supervision and direct support—account for at least 80% of their total compensated services during the taxable year, 100% of that employee's annual Form W-2 wages qualify as QREs.

First, regarding the post-2024 statutory restructure between IRC § 174A and IRC § 174, prior rules under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA, Pub. L. 115-97, § 13206) mandated 5-year capitalization and amortization for domestic R&E expenditures and 15-year amortization for foreign R&E expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. On July 4, 2025, Congress enacted Public Law 119-21 (139 Stat. 72, the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act or OBBBA), Title VII, § 70302, effective for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Public Law 119-21 enacted IRC § 174A, restoring immediate full expensing under § 174A(a) (or elective amortization over not less than 60 months under § 174A(c)) for domestic R&E expenditures, updated IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) to cross-reference § 174A, and restricted mandatory 15-year capitalization under amended IRC § 174 exclusively to foreign R&E expenditures. Second, regarding regulatory citation precision, the phrase "all such costs incident to the development or improvement of a product" and the definition of "product" appear in 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) and (a)(3) rather than the statutory text of IRC §§ 174 or 174A. Similarly, the definitions of "engaging in qualified research," "direct supervision," and "direct support" are codified in IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(1)–(3), whereas 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2) governs the 80% "substantially all" wage threshold.

Third, a strict "first-line management" limitation governs direct supervision: while taxpayers often seek to claim department heads, vice presidents, Chief Technology Officers (CTOs), and Chief Financial Officers (CFOs) performing strategic review, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2) restricts "direct supervision" to immediate supervision (first-line management) of qualified research and explicitly excludes "supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line managers report, even if that manager is a qualified research scientist". In Scott Moore, et al. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-20, the U.S. Tax Court disallowed 100% of a Chief Operating Officer's claimed wages because he was two management layers removed from the researchers and lacked documentation of direct hands-on performance. Furthermore, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) explicitly excludes "officers engaged in supervising financial or personnel matters" from direct support. Fourth, although 26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)(1)–(2) provides that expenses incurred prior to commencing a new business are generally not paid or incurred "in carrying on a trade or business" under IRC § 41(b)(1), IRC § 41(b)(4) establishes an explicit statutory exception for in-house research expenses (including I2D wages and supplies) of startup ventures if the taxpayer's principal purpose is to use the research results in the active conduct of a future trade or business. Fifth, practitioners must distinguish between tax regulations (26 CFR § 1.41-2), federal grant rules (2 CFR § 200.413), and facility allocation rules: university federal grant guidance (2 CFR § 200.413) and IRS Notice 2023-63 square-footage or headcount allocation rules for § 174 overhead cannot be used to attribute general administrative labor or general laboratory janitorial cleaning to § 41 QREs. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3), cleaning equipment used in qualified research qualifies as direct support, whereas a janitor's general cleaning of a research laboratory is excluded as general and administrative (G&A) overhead, and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1) requires employee wages to be allocated based on each employee's actual time ratio of qualified services to total services. Sixth, in computing the 80% wage cliff for a first-line CTO spending 10% of their time on direct research, 70% on direct supervision (totaling 80% qualified services), and 20% on G&A, reducing G&A to 19% would yield 81% qualified services (100% minus 19%); for total qualified services to fall to 79% and trigger the cliff loss of the G&A wage buffer, non-qualified G&A time must increase to 21% (10% direct research plus 69% direct supervision equals 79% qualified services).
I. The Strategic Nexus of Incident to Development (I2D)
A. Definitional Mechanism and Statutory Evolution (IRC §§ 174, 174A, and 41)

In federal R&D tax analysis, Incident to Development (I2D) describes the regulatory mechanism through which research-related support, supervisory, and indirect costs are captured for federal tax purposes. The foundational phrase originates in Treasury Regulation (26 CFR) § 1.174-2(a)(1) (as amended by T.D. 9680, 79 FR 42193, effective July 21, 2014), which defines "research or experimental expenditures" as expenditures incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business that represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense, and states that the term "generally includes all such costs incident to the development or improvement of a product". Under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(3), the term "product" is defined broadly to include "any pilot model, process, formula, invention, technique, patent, or similar property," whether held for sale, lease, or license, or used in the taxpayer's own trade or business. In addition, IRC § 174(c)(3) and IRC § 174A(d)(3) provide by statute that any amount paid or incurred in connection with the development of software shall be treated as a research or experimental expenditure.

To evaluate how I2D operates under current law, practitioners must account for the major legislative restructuring enacted after the TCJA amortization period. Under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Pub. L. 115-97, § 13206, enacted December 22, 2017), for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, taxpayers were prohibited from immediately deducting "specified research or experimental" (SRE) expenditures under former IRC § 174(a)(1) and were required to capitalize and amortize them ratably over 5 years (60 months) for domestic research and 15 years (180 months) for foreign research, starting at the midpoint of the taxable year in which the expenditures were paid or incurred.

On July 4, 2025, Public Law 119-21 (139 Stat. 72, § 70302) bifurcated the statutory treatment of domestic and foreign R&E expenditures for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Newly enacted IRC § 174A(a) allows taxpayers to immediately deduct domestic R&E expenditures in the taxable year paid or incurred (notwithstanding IRC § 263), or alternatively to elect under IRC § 174A(c) to charge domestic R&E expenditures (that are chargeable to capital account but not subject to depreciation under IRC § 167 or depletion under IRC § 611) to capital account and amortize them ratably over a period of not less than 60 months beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realizes benefits from such expenditures. Transition rules under Public Law 119-21 § 70302(f) and IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-28 (2025-38 I.R.B. 393, released August 28, 2025, modifying Rev. Proc. 2025-23) implement automatic accounting method changes (applied on a cut-off basis without an IRC § 481(a) adjustment for post-2024 domestic expenditures) and permit taxpayers under OBBBA § 70302(f)(2)(B) to recover remaining unamortized 2022–2024 domestic SRE amounts either in full in the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, or ratably over a two-taxable-year period beginning with that year. Additionally, under OBBBA § 70302(f)(1)(C), eligible small businesses (meeting the IRC § 448(c) gross receipts test for their first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, and not classified as tax shelters) may elect retroactive application of IRC § 174A back to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. Public Law 119-21 also amended IRC § 280C(c)(1) to require reducing domestic R&E deductions or capitalized amounts under § 174A by the amount of the IRC § 41(a) research credit unless the taxpayer timely makes the irrevocable reduced credit election under IRC § 280C(c)(2). Conversely, amended IRC § 174(a)–(b) applies exclusively to foreign research or experimental expenditures (attributable to research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or U.S. territories or possessions within the meaning of IRC § 41(d)(4)(F)), which remain subject to mandatory capitalization and 15-year ratable amortization, with IRC § 174(d) prohibiting any immediate deduction or reduction to amount realized upon the disposition, retirement, or abandonment of foreign R&E property after May 12, 2025.

In the context of the IRC § 41 Credit for Increasing Research Activities, qualifying under IRC § 174A (for post-2024 domestic research, or IRC § 174 for prior years) is the first of four statutory tests for "qualified research" under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A), alongside the requirements under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)–(C) that the research be undertaken to discover information that is technological in nature, be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer, and have substantially all of its activities constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose (new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A)). Even when an activity satisfies the four-part test of IRC § 41(d), a cost incurred incident to that activity is eligible for the tax credit only if it falls within the statutory categories of Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) under IRC § 41(b). Because IRC § 41(b) excludes general and administrative (G&A) overhead, facility rent, ordinary utilities, and equipment depreciation, the primary mechanism for capturing I2D costs in the § 41 credit calculation is the inclusion of "direct supervision" and "direct support" labor within "qualified services" under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2)–(3).
B. Core Regulatory Thesis: The Wage Multiplier and IRS Scrutiny

The financial significance of I2D in IRC § 41 stems from the interaction between the definition of qualified services (IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)) and the "substantially all" rule for wages (26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2)). Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1), if an employee performs both qualified services and non-qualified services during the taxable year, only the portion of taxable W-2 wages allocated to qualified services (by default, the ratio of hours spent performing qualified services to total hours worked across all services) constitutes an in-house research expense. However, under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) (flush language) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2), if at least 80% of an employee's compensated services during the taxable year consist of qualified services—combining hands-on research, first-line direct supervision, and direct support—then 100% of that employee's wages for the taxable year qualify as QREs.

Without the inclusion of direct supervision and direct support under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)(ii), first-line R&D managers, lead engineers who review technical protocols, and specialized technicians or machinists who fabricate experimental models would have their credit-eligible wages restricted to the hours they personally conduct hands-on experiments—frequently dropping them below the 80% threshold and forfeiting the 20% non-qualified wage buffer. In a representative financial model, properly identifying and substantiating I2D direct supervision and direct support wages adds $350,000 (a 35.0% lift) to a $1,000,000 core engineering wage base, expanding total QREs to $1,350,000. Because supervisory and support wages carry high dollar values and rely on functional time allocations rather than pure laboratory bench work, the IRS subjects I2D wage claims to heightened examination scrutiny, requiring contemporaneous factual substantiation of both the "direct" nexus and the 80% time threshold.
II. Regulatory Genesis and Definitional Boundaries of I2D
A. The Foundation in IRC §§ 174 and 174A and 26 CFR § 1.174-2

Under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1), expenditures represent R&E costs in the experimental or laboratory sense if they are incurred for activities intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product. Uncertainty exists when the information available to the taxpayer does not establish either: (1) the capability or method for developing or improving the product, or (2) the appropriate design of the product. Eligibility under § 174 and § 174A depends on the nature of the activity to which the expenditures relate rather than the nature of the product or its degree of technological advancement, and the ultimate success, failure, sale, or internal use of the product is irrelevant. Costs may qualify under § 174 or § 174A even if paid or incurred after production begins, provided they are incurred before uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of the product is eliminated, and if uncertainty does not exist at the overall product level, eligibility is evaluated at the component or subcomponent level under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(5).

Because 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) captures "all such costs incident to the development or improvement of a product," its scope extends beyond immediate laboratory experimentation to include three key categories of incidental expenditures. First, under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(4), it covers pilot models, defined as any representation or model of a product (including a fully functional model or component under § 1.174-2(a)(5)) produced to evaluate and resolve technical uncertainty concerning the product during development or improvement. Second, under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) and IRS Notice 2023-63, § 4.03(1)(d), it includes patent application and perfection costs, explicitly encompassing "attorneys' fees expended in making and perfecting a patent application". Third, under IRC §§ 174(c)(1) and 174A(d)(1) and Notice 2023-63, § 4.03(1)(c), while capital expenditures to acquire or improve land or depreciable or depletable property are excluded, annual depreciation, amortization, or depletion allowances (under IRC §§ 167 and 611) on property used in the performance of, or in direct support of, R&E activities are treated as R&E expenditures, alongside allocable overhead incident to research (such as facility rent, utilities, property taxes, and security or maintenance of research spaces).

However, 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(2) and (a)(6) and IRS Notice 2023-63, § 4.03(2) establish strict outer boundaries that exclude specific activities and costs from being treated as "incident to development" even under the broad §§ 174/174A standard. Under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(2), except as provided in the component rule of paragraph (a)(5), costs paid or incurred in the production of a product after uncertainty concerning its development or improvement has been eliminated are ineligible production costs. Furthermore, 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i)–(vii) explicitly excludes seven categories of expenditures from R&E treatment:

items: The ordinary testing or inspection of materials or products for quality control (defined in § 1.174-2(a)(7) as testing or inspection to determine whether particular units of materials or products conform to specified parameters, although testing to determine if the product design is appropriate is not quality control testing);
The acquisition of another's patent, model, production, or process; and
Research in connection with literary, historical, or similar projects.

body.text: In addition, general and administrative (G&A) expenses that relate to a corporation's activities as a whole and do not contribute directly to the R&E effort (such as routine payroll processing and accounting department functions) are excluded, as are severance compensation and interest on debt used to finance operations and research (Notice 2023-63, § 4.03(2)(a)–(b)), as well as Voluntary Separation Program (VSP) severance payments (IRS Chief Counsel Advice 20131102F, dated February 8, 2013, holding that VSP payments calculated on multi-year tenure during a workforce reduction are neither experimental costs under § 174 nor nexus-supported wages under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1)).
B. Bridging IRC §§ 174/174A and IRC § 41: The "Carrying On a Trade or Business" Requirement and Startup Exception

To transition from an R&E expenditure under IRC § 174A (or § 174) to a credit-eligible QRE under IRC § 41(b)(1), the expenditure must be paid or incurred by the taxpayer "in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer". As stated in 26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)(1), the phrase "in carrying on a trade or business" has the same narrower meaning for purposes of IRC § 41(b)(1) as it has for IRC § 162 (ordinary and necessary business expenses), rather than the broader "in connection with a trade or business" standard of IRC §§ 174 and 174A. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)(2), expenses paid or incurred prior to commencing a new business (as distinguished from expanding an existing business) are not paid or incurred in carrying on a trade or business under the general regulatory rule.

Crucially, however, IRC § 41(b)(4) (Trade or business requirement disregarded for in-house research expenses of certain startup ventures) explicitly overrides this limitation for in-house research expenses. Under IRC § 41(b)(4)(A)–(B), a taxpayer is treated as meeting the trade or business requirement of § 41(b)(1) with respect to in-house research expenses (wages for qualified services, tangible supplies, and eligible computer time-sharing) if, at the time the expenses are paid or incurred, the taxpayer's principal purpose in making the expenditures is to use the results of the research in the active conduct of a future trade or business of the taxpayer, or of one or more other persons who with the taxpayer are treated as a single taxpayer under the controlled-group aggregation rules of IRC § 41(f)(1). By contrast, contract research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(3) are not covered by the § 41(b)(4) startup exception and remain subject to the active-business rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)(1)–(2).

Additionally, under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)(1) and (a)(3)(i), if a taxpayer performs research on behalf of another person and retains no substantial rights in the research results, or incurs contract research expenses where the product or result of the research is intended to be transferred to another in return for license or royalty payments without the taxpayer using the product in its own trade or business, the expenses are ineligible for the § 41 credit.
C. Strategic Divergence: Dual-Track Accounting for Incidental Costs

A central compliance challenge is the divergence between the expansive scope of incidental costs included under IRC §§ 174 and 174A and the restrictive scope of QREs under IRC § 41(b). As IRS Notice 2023-63 specifies, rules addressing indirect costs incident to SRE activities under § 174 do not alter the eligibility or computation rules for QREs under IRC § 41. Under IRC § 41(b)(1)–(3) and the IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG), if an expense is not explicitly enumerated in § 41(b)—namely: (1) employee wages for qualified services under § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), (2) tangible non-depreciable supplies used in qualified research under § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), (3) qualified off-premises time-sharing computer usage fees under § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii), or (4) 65% (or 75% for qualified research consortia under § 41(b)(3)(C), or 100% for eligible energy research under § 41(b)(3)(D)) of qualified contract research—a taxpayer may not claim the expense as a QRE.

While a taxpayer must track and allocate depreciation on laboratory equipment and facilities, facility rent, property taxes, ordinary utilities, and patent attorney fees for purposes of IRC § 174A domestic deductions (or IRC § 174 capitalization), every one of those indirect cost categories is barred from the IRC § 41 QRE base. This requires corporate tax departments to maintain a dual-track accounting architecture: a broad cost-allocation system capturing all direct and indirect costs incident to R&E for IRC §§ 174/174A compliance (maintained consistently across subtitle A of the Code per Notice 2023-63, § 4.04), and a narrow, employee- and supply-specific filter for IRC § 41 credit claims.
III. Incident to Development in QRE Maximization: The Wage Component
A. Defining Qualified Services: Engaging, Direct Supervision, and Direct Support

For employee compensation to qualify as an in-house research expense under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), the payment must constitute "wages" as defined by IRC § 41(b)(2)(D) and § 3401(a)—taxable wages subject to federal income tax withholding as reported on Form W-2, including bonuses and taxable stock option exercises (where the IRS ATG directs examiners to look to the grant year to verify whether the underlying services were qualified services and include the option spread in the exercise year), as well as earned income of self-employed individuals under IRC § 401(c)(1)–(2), while excluding non-taxed fringe benefits, employer FICA/FUTA payroll taxes, and wages used for the IRC § 51(a) Work Opportunity Tax Credit—and must be paid or incurred for "qualified services" performed by the employee.

Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B), the statutory definition of qualified services is bipartite, encompassing: (i) engaging in qualified research, or (ii) engaging in the direct supervision or direct support of research activities which constitute qualified research. Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c)(1)–(3) defines these three functional categories with strict operational boundaries. First, under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(1), "engaging in qualified research" means the "actual conduct of qualified research (as in the case of a scientist conducting laboratory experiments)". Second, under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2), "direct supervision" means the "immediate supervision (first-line management) of qualified research (as in the case of a research scientist who directly supervises laboratory experiments, but who may not actually perform experiments)". Crucially, the regulation establishes a bright-line exclusion: "'Direct supervision' does not include supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line managers report, even if that manager is a qualified research scientist". In Scott Moore, et al. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-20, the taxpayers claimed 65% of the wages of their S corporation's Chief Operating Officer (COO) as QREs. Although the COO oversaw the R&D department and possessed technical responsibilities, the Tax Court found that the Senior VP of Engineering—not the COO—was the direct supervisor of the R&D personnel. Because the COO was two management layers removed from the researchers (violating the "one-up" first-line management rule of § 1.41-2(c)(2)) and lacked documentation proving hands-on technical experimentation, the Tax Court disallowed 100% of the COO's wages. Third, under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3), "direct support" means services in the direct support of either (i) persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research, or (ii) persons who are directly supervising persons engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research. Direct support does not include supervision.

To demarcate eligible direct support from ineligible general and administrative (G&A) overhead, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) provides four explicit qualifying examples and four explicit non-qualifying examples (which remain excluded whether the administrative personnel are housed inside the R&D department or in a separate corporate department):

cells: Machinist machining a part of an experimental model used in qualified research (or fabricating a custom prototype engine casing)
Directly fabricates physical experimental apparatus required by researchers to test design uncertainty.
Laboratory Worker cleaning equipment used in qualified research
Directly maintains and prepares the specific testing equipment used in experiments.
Directly organizes experimental data generated by or for the research team.
Secretary typing reports describing laboratory results derived from qualified research
Directly documents experimental findings for the researchers or their immediate supervisors.
VP of Engineering / R&D Manager participating in technical design reviews to critique architecture and direct researchers
Qualifies only to the extent the manager is directly engaging in technical problem-solving or acting as first-line supervisor of the researchers, not supervising via intermediate managers.
Janitor performing general cleaning of a research laboratory
General facility cleaning benefits the building/environment indirectly rather than preparing specific experimental apparatus.
Payroll Clerk preparing salary checks for laboratory scientists
Routine corporate payroll administration; only indirectly benefits research activities.
Financial tracking and tax/book accounting do not contribute to resolving technical uncertainty.
HR Director / Corporate Officers interviewing/hiring R&D staff or supervising financial or personnel matters
Explicitly excluded by § 1.41-2(c)(3), even if the personnel or officers belong to the research division.

body.text: B. The Critical 80% "Substantially All" Rule for Wages (26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2))

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1) and the IRS Audit Techniques Guide, in the absence of another allocation method that the taxpayer can demonstrate to be more appropriate, the amount of in-house research wage expense for an employee who performs both qualified and non-qualified services is determined by multiplying the employee's total annual W-2 wages by the ratio of the total time actually spent by the employee performing qualified services to the total time spent performing all services for the taxpayer during the taxable year (excluding non-working time such as sick leave from the fraction).

However, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2) implements the statutory "substantially all" rule of IRC § 41(b)(2)(B). If the wages allocated to qualified services (under the time-ratio basis of § 1.41-2(d)(1)) constitute at least 80% of the wages paid to or incurred for the employee during the taxable year, then "qualified services" means all of the services performed by the employee for the taxpayer during the taxable year—allowing 100% of that employee's W-2 wages to be claimed as QREs. This determination is performed on an employee-by-employee basis.
C. Audit Defense Distinction: Process of Experimentation (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6)) vs. Qualified Services (26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2))

As confirmed in the Treasury Regulations and the IRS Audit Techniques Guide, taxpayers and examiners must maintain a strict conceptual and computational separation between two distinct 80% "substantially all" rules under IRC § 41. In the first step—the activity- or project-level "substantially all" rule for Process of Experimentation under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6)—for a business component's research activities to constitute "qualified research," 80% or more of the taxpayer's research activities with respect to that discrete business component, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, must constitute elements of a process of experimentation (identifying technical uncertainty, identifying alternatives, and conducting an evaluative process such as modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error relying on physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science) for a qualified purpose under IRC § 41(d)(3) (new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality). In the second step—the employee-level "substantially all" rule for wages under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2)—only after a business component satisfies the four-part test (including the ≥80% Process of Experimentation test under § 1.41-4(a)(6)) does the taxpayer apply the employee-level wage test of § 1.41-2(d)(2) to determine whether an individual employee spent ≥80% of their compensated time performing qualified services (engaging in, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research).

Crucially, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) explicitly mandates that the 80% Process of Experimentation test is measured "(and without regard to section 1.41-2(d)(2))". This prevents circular bootstrapping: a taxpayer cannot use the 20% non-qualified G&A buffer of an 80%+ employee under § 1.41-2(d)(2) to inflate the numerator of the project-level Process of Experimentation test under § 1.41-4(a)(6). Conversely, if a business component satisfies the ≥80% Process of Experimentation test, the remaining balance (20% or less) of research activities on that business component may still qualify as part of the qualified research effort provided those activities satisfy IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) (eligibility under § 174 or § 174A) and are not explicitly excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4). Furthermore, as the Seventh Circuit held in Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), pilot model production expenses that qualify under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(4) must be included in the denominator of the 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) "substantially all" fraction.
D. Hypothetical Worked Examples and Role-By-Role QRE Leverage Analysis
To illustrate the exact operation and cliff effect of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1)–(2), we audit and recompute the hypothetical employee scenarios below.
Step-by-Step Recomputation of the Hypothetical CTO Cliff Example

Suppose a hypothetical Chief Technology Officer (CTO) earns $300,000 in annual W-2 wages and is responsible for a division developing a new manufacturing process that satisfies the four-part test of IRC § 41(d). Crucially, to satisfy 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2) and Moore v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2023-20), assume this CTO acts directly as the first-line manager of the experimental engineering team rather than supervising through intermediate managers.

In Scenario A (Baseline — Meets 80% Threshold), the CTO's documented annual time allocation consists of 10% engaging in hands-on prototype testing (§ 1.41-2(c)(1)), 70% in first-line direct supervision reviewing technical design specifications, directing experimental goals, and approving alternative methodologies (§ 1.41-2(c)(2)), and 20% in corporate strategic planning and quarterly shareholder reporting (Non-Qualified G&A). Summing the qualified components yields Total Qualified Services of 10% + 70% = 80%, with total accounted time of 80% + 20% = 100%. Because 80% meets the ≥80% threshold under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2), the "substantially all" safe harbor is satisfied, and 100% of the CTO's wages ($300,000) qualify as QREs—capturing the $60,000 (20%) G&A portion inside the QRE base alongside the $240,000 (80%) of direct and supervisory wages.

In Scenario B (Cliff Failure — Exact Mathematical Mechanics), if non-qualified G&A time were 19%, total qualified services would be 100% − 19% = 81%, which would still satisfy the ≥80% threshold and yield 100% QRE inclusion. For the CTO's qualified services to fall by 1 percentage point to 79%, non-qualified G&A time must increase by 1 percentage point from 20% to 21% (specifically, 10% hands-on prototype testing + 69% first-line direct supervision = 79% qualified services, and 21% G&A = 100% total time). Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1)–(2), because 79% is below the 80% threshold, the taxpayer loses the "substantially all" safe harbor and may claim only the pro-rata 79% of the CTO's wages ($237,000 of $300,000)—a $63,000 QRE reduction caused by a single percentage point shift in time allocation.
Summary Table of Hypothetical Employee Scenarios Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)–(d)

headers: Time Incident to Development: DS / DSU (§ 1.41-2(c)(2)–(3))

cells: 79% — Fails 80% threshold; limited to pro-rata ratio under § 1.41-2(d)(1).
100% — High direct support focus (equipment prep/data compilation) meets ≥80% rule.

body.text: IV. Application of I2D to Supplies and Indirect Costs
A. Qualified Supplies (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), § 41(b)(2)(C), and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b))

While wages represent the primary vehicle for I2D optimization under IRC § 41, the concept of incidental development materials also applies to supplies, albeit under strict statutory constraints. Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), in-house research expenses include "any amount paid or incurred for supplies used in the conduct of qualified research". IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) defines the term "supplies" as "any tangible property other than—(i) land or improvements to land, and (ii) property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation".

Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(b)(1) explicitly connects the eligibility of supplies to the performance of qualified services (which includes direct supervision and direct support under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)):

"Supplies and personal property (except to the extent provided in paragraph (b)(4) of this section) are used in the conduct of qualified research if they are used in the performance of qualified services (as defined in section 41(b)(2)(B), but without regard to the last sentence thereof) by an employee of the taxpayer (or by a person acting in a capacity similar to that of an employee of the taxpayer; see example (6) of § 1.41-2(e)(5))."

This regulatory provision establishes two critical rules for I2D supplies. First, tangible, non-depreciable materials—such as raw metal stock used by a machinist (direct support) to fabricate an experimental prototype component, or chemical reagents, test tubes, beakers, and consumables used by a laboratory technician in experimental setup and testing—qualify as QRE supplies because they are used in the performance of qualified services under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)(i)–(ii). However, as the IRS Audit Techniques Guide cautions, examiners closely scrutinize substantial "prototype" supply claims to verify that the prototype is not (and does not contain) property of a character subject to an allowance for depreciation. Second, the parenthetical in 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(1)—"(as defined in section 41(b)(2)(B), but without regard to the last sentence thereof)"—means that the 80% "substantially all" rule of IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) applies only to wages, not to supplies. Even if an employee spends 85% of their time on qualified services (so that 100% of their wages qualify), any supplies consumed by that employee during their remaining 15% non-qualified/G&A activities do not qualify as QRE supplies.
B. Exclusion of General Overhead, Depreciation, and Facility Maintenance

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(1) and the IRS Audit Techniques Guide, expenditures for supplies or personal property that represent indirect research expenditures or general and administrative (G&A) expenses do not qualify as in-house research expenses. Although depreciation allowances on research equipment and facilities are included as R&E expenditures under IRC §§ 174(c)(1) and 174A(d)(1) and Notice 2023-63, § 4.03(1)(c), depreciable property is barred from the definition of supplies under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii). Similarly, under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(4) and the Instructions for Form 6765, amounts paid for the use or lease of personal property are disallowed as QREs, except for amounts paid or incurred to another person under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) for the right to use (time-sharing) computers in the conduct of qualified research, provided the computer is owned and operated by someone other than the taxpayer, located off the taxpayer's premises, and the taxpayer is not the primary user or operator of the computer.

With respect to facility overhead, under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(2)(i) and the IRS Audit Techniques Guide, amounts paid or incurred for utilities such as water, electricity, and natural gas used in the building where qualified research is performed are treated as G&A expenses and excluded from QREs, along with facility rent, telephone expenses, travel, meals, entertainment, relocation, professional dues, and royalty or license expenses. However, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii) provides a narrow exception for extraordinary utility expenditures: to the extent the taxpayer can establish that the special character of the qualified research required additional extraordinary expenditures for utilities (for example, high-energy electricity required to operate laser or nuclear research equipment, as opposed to general laboratory lighting), the additional expenditure is treated as a supply used in the conduct of qualified research.

Finally, practitioners must distinguish university federal grant guidance summarizing 2 CFR § 200.413 (Office of Management and Budget Uniform Guidance for federal awards)—under which administrative and clerical salaries normally treated as indirect Facilities and Administrative (F&A) costs may be directly charged to a federal grant if the services are "integral" to a project, specifically identified with the project, and not double-recovered as indirect costs—from the rules governing the IRC § 41 tax credit. First, 2 CFR § 200.413 governs federal grant cost accounting, not the Internal Revenue Code; for the IRC § 41 tax credit, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) governs and restricts administrative or clerical eligibility strictly to tasks that directly support researchers or first-line supervisors (such as typing laboratory result reports or compiling research data). Second, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3) draws a sharp line between a "laboratory worker for cleaning equipment used in qualified research" (which is Direct Support) and a "janitor for general cleaning of a research laboratory" (which is explicitly excluded as G&A). Thus, a lab technician spending 85% of their time cleaning and maintaining experimental apparatus and equipment counts toward the 80% Direct Support threshold, whereas general cleaning of the laboratory facility or environment does not.
V. Compliance Imperatives: Substantiation, Procedural Specificity, and Cost Allocation
A. Factual Substantiation of Actual Activities vs. Job Titles

The IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities (i.e. Research Tax Credit) IRC § 41 - Qualified Research Expenses (updated July 2, 2026) establishes an unambiguous examination standard for employee wages:

"Determinations as to whether an employee is (or is not) engaged in qualified services must not be based solely on job descriptions or titles. Credit eligibility is based solely upon what an employee actually does, or does not, do during a specific time period."

While an employee's technical education and professional credentials are noted during an audit, they are not conclusive evidence that the employee performed qualified services. Moreover, the IRS instructs examiners to focus audit resources on employees whose job descriptions suggest non-qualifying functions—such as administration, executive management, manufacturing, or marketing—and to use employee interviews to supplement and corroborate existing records.

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d) (T.D. 9104), the taxpayer bears the burden of retaining records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that claimed expenditures are eligible for the credit. As demonstrated in Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287, 308 (7th Cir. Mar. 7, 2023), aff'g T.C. Memo. 2021-15, where a taxpayer relies on generalized estimates and fails to maintain activity-level documentation proving time and costs spent on a process of experimentation, courts will disallow the credit in full ("Section 41(d) requires us to walk by sight, not by faith") and refuse to apply the Cohan estimation rule or the "shrinking-back" rule (26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2)) to smaller subcomponents. Contemporaneous evidence used to substantiate I2D direct supervision and direct support includes W-2 payroll records, electronic time-tracking logs, project calendars and appointment books, performance evaluations, engineering design review minutes, and functional interviews corroborating the nexus between the support or supervisory employee and specific business components.
B. Procedural Specificity Under 26 CFR § 301.6402-2(b)(1) and Refund Claim Jurisprudence
IRS enforcement has increasingly targeted procedural specificity at the time of filing, relying on 26 CFR § 301.6402-2(b)(1):

"No refund or credit will be allowed after the expiration of the statutory period of limitation applicable to the filing of a claim therefor except upon one or more of the grounds set forth in a claim filed before the expiration of such period. The claim must set forth in detail each ground upon which a credit or refund is claimed and facts sufficient to apprise the Commissioner of the exact basis thereof. The statement of the grounds and facts must be verified by a written declaration that it is made under the penalties of perjury. A claim which does not comply with this paragraph will not be considered for any purpose as a claim for refund or credit."

Two federal court decisions—Harper v. United States and Premier Tech, Inc. v. United States—catalyzed the IRS's current disclosure regime for § 41 claims. In Harper v. United States, No. 3:18-cv-02110-DMS-LL, 2019 WL 1877185 (S.D. Cal. Apr. 25, 2019), rev'd, No. 19-55933, 847 Fed. App'x 408, 2021 WL 732970 (9th Cir. Feb. 25, 2021), the taxpayers filed amended returns claiming § 41 research credits for tax years 2008 and 2010 and produced over 100,000 pages of documentation (112,000 pages per the concurrence) during a four-year IRS examination. After the IRS denied the claim on the merits and the taxpayers sued in federal district court, the government moved to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction under IRC § 7422(a), arguing that the initial Form 6765 filings failed to set forth detailed facts under 26 CFR § 301.6402-2(b)(1). The Southern District of California dismissed the suit. On appeal, the Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that while compliance with § 301.6402-2(b)(1) is an administrative exhaustion prerequisite, the IRS unmistakably waived its procedural objection by conducting a four-year substantive audit directed at the merits of the research credit and issuing a final determination on the merits.

In Premier Tech, Inc. v. United States, No. 2:20-cv-00890-TS-CMR (D. Utah July 15, 2021)—decided on July 15, 2021, one day before Intermountain Electronics, Inc. v. United States, No. 2:20-cv-00501 (D. Utah July 16, 2021), notwithstanding a secondary source typographical reference to "7/15/22"—the government moved to dismiss the taxpayer's amended-return refund suit under 26 CFR § 301.6402-2(b)(1) because the filing did not attach project-by-project narratives or component-level wage and supply breakdowns. Without relying on waiver, the U.S. District Court for the District of Utah denied the government's motion to dismiss, holding that the taxpayer satisfied § 301.6402-2(b)(1) at the time by attaching a completed Form 6765 specifying claimed wages, supplies, base amounts, and credit calculations.

In direct response to its losses in Harper and Premier Tech, the IRS issued Chief Counsel Advice 20214101F and News Release IR-2021-203 on October 15, 2021, followed by LB&I Interim Guidance Memorandum LB&I-04-1222-0026. To prevent courts from finding that the IRS waived § 301.6402-2(b)(1) by auditing a claim, Chief Counsel instructed the IRS to screen and reject deficient refund claims (issuing Letter 6428 for perfection and Letter 6430 for "no consideration") before initiating an examination. Beginning January 10, 2022, the IRS required taxpayers filing § 41 refund claims on amended returns (or Administrative Adjustment Requests for BBA partnerships) to provide five items of information at filing verified under penalties of perjury (with a 45-day perfection window during a transition period subsequently extended through January 10, 2027):

items: Identify all business components to which the § 41 claim relates for that year;
For each business component, identify all research activities performed;
Identify all individuals who performed each research activity (by first and last name or by title/position);
Identify the information each individual sought to discover; and
Provide total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year (which may be done using Form 6765).

body.text: On June 18, 2024, the IRS updated its refund claim guidance (FAQ 21) to waive Items 3 and 4 at the time of filing (the names of the individuals and the specific information each individual sought to discover), while retaining Items 1, 2, and 5 as mandatory upfront disclosures for all valid refund claims and reserving the right to request Items 3 and 4 during an audit.
C. Cost Allocation Methodologies: IRS Notice 2023-63 vs. 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1)

Practitioners must carefully distinguish between the allocation rules governing IRC §§ 174 and 174A R&E expenditures under IRS Notice 2023-63 and the employee wage allocation rule governing IRC § 41 QREs under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1). Issued on September 8, 2023 (2023-39 I.R.B. 919) and clarified by Notice 2024-12 (2024-5 I.R.B. 616), Section 4.03(3) of Notice 2023-63 requires taxpayers to allocate indirect and incidental costs to SRE activities based on a cause-and-effect relationship between the costs and the SRE activities, or another relationship that reasonably relates the costs to the benefits provided to the SRE activities. In Section 4.03(4) of Notice 2023-63, using the example of "Company A" (which incurs $200,000 of building depreciation on a 10,000-square-foot facility housing a 5,000 sq. ft. Manufacturing department and five 1,000 sq. ft. departments for Research, Engineering, Legal, Personnel, and Accounting), the IRS approves allocating facility depreciation to SRE activities by multiplying the relative square footage occupied by the Research, Engineering, and Legal departments by the percentage of time employees in those departments spend on or directly supporting SRE activities, and allocating equipment and computer depreciation ($150,000 in Research, $100,000 in Engineering, and $20,000 in Legal) based on the proportion of total labor hours or time spent on research activities.

However, Section 4.03(3) of Notice 2023-63 explicitly cautions that an allocation method that satisfies Section 4.03(3) for § 174 may not be appropriate for allocating that same type of cost under other sections of the Internal Revenue Code. For the IRC § 41 tax credit, general facility overhead and depreciation are excluded altogether, and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1) mandates that unless the taxpayer demonstrates another method to be more appropriate, an employee's qualified wages must be determined by multiplying the employee's W-2 wages by "the ratio of the total time actually spent by the employee in the performance of qualified services for the taxpayer to the total time spent by the employee in the performance of all services for the taxpayer during the taxable year". Therefore, while departmental time-tracking and specific activity identification are compliant with § 1.41-2(d)(1), a taxpayer cannot allocate an administrative or support employee's wages to the § 41 credit using building square footage or company-wide headcount ratios.
VI. Strategic Recommendations: Proactive Compliance and Form 6765 Section G Execution

Grounded in the statutory and regulatory rules above, corporate tax departments seeking to maximize and defend I2D wages and supplies under IRC § 41 should implement a three-pillar compliance protocol.
A. Formalizing Internal I2D Policies Around the "One-Up" and Direct Support Rules

Taxpayers should establish an internal R&D tax compliance manual that defines Direct Supervision and Direct Support strictly in accordance with 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2)–(3) rather than relying on corporate job titles or organizational charts. For every manager or executive whose wages are claimed under Direct Supervision, the compliance manual should require documenting the exact reporting chain proving they are the immediate ("one-up") supervisor of the engineers or scientists conducting the experimentation, or documenting their direct hands-on technical contributions, thereby avoiding the second-tier management disallowance of Moore v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2023-20). Similarly, for technicians, machinists, lab workers, and administrative support personnel, policies should explicitly map claimed hours to qualifying activities under § 1.41-2(c)(3) (machining prototype components, cleaning experimental equipment, compiling test data, or typing laboratory reports) while carving out general facility janitorial work, payroll, HR, and accounting.
B. Granular, Contemporaneous Time-Tracking Aligned With Form 6765 Section G

Redesigned Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities)—specifically Section G (Business Component Information)—requires taxpayers to report qualified employee wages broken down into three discrete columns per business component: Column 50 for the direct conduct of qualified research, Column 51 for direct supervision (first-line management), and Column 52 for direct support (alongside computer lease costs in Column 55 and contract research expenses in Column 56, as well as entity and component identifiers in Columns 49(a)–(f)). Per the Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025), Section G is optional for all filers on original returns for taxable years beginning before 2026, and becomes mandatory for taxable years beginning after 2025. Section G is excused only if the taxpayer is: (1) a qualified small business (under IRC § 41(h)(3)) electing the reduced payroll tax credit, or (2) filing an original return where controlled-group total QREs are $1.5 million or less and average annual gross receipts for the prior three tax years (under IRC § 448(c)(3)) are $50 million or less. Filers required to complete Section G must report component-by-component QRE breakdowns in descending order of size covering at least 80% of total QREs, up to a maximum of 50 business components, aggregating any remaining components under a single "Aggregate Business Components" entry in Column 49(c) (and if statistical sampling is used, appending "sample" in Column 49(c) and attaching Form6765StatSamplePlan.pdf).

To comply with both 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1)–(2) and Form 6765 Section G Columns 50–52, companies should configure electronic time-tracking systems so that R&D and technical support staff log hours by specific business component across four discrete activity codes: (i) Engaging in Qualified Research (Column 50), (ii) Direct Supervision — First-Line (Column 51), (iii) Direct Support (Column 52), and (iv) Non-Qualified / G&A.
C. Upfront Substantiation Memoranda for Original and Amended Filings

When filing an amended return or refund claim including an IRC § 41 credit, taxpayers must complete Column 49(f) of Form 6765 where applicable and attach the required specificity disclosures under 26 CFR § 301.6402-2(b)(1) and the IRS's refund claim procedures—identifying every business component, the research activities performed for each component, and the total qualified wage, supply, and contract research expenses. In parallel, taxpayers should prepare a contemporaneous technical and computational memorandum detailing the employee-by-employee 80% "substantially all" calculations under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2) and verifying that the project-level 80% Process of Experimentation test under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) was satisfied prior to applying the § 1.41-2(d)(2) wage rule.
